section_summary: This section continues a discussion of Japanese seismology, then presents enclosures on inventions, industrial research, engineering, patent statistics, household budgets, and national wealth. Several enclosures reproduce or translate published articles and statistical tables from the 1930s.

subfiles.title: Statement Regarding Japanese Work in Seismology
subfiles.about: The statement describes Japanese contributions to seismology and their influence abroad.
subfiles.summary: Credits Japanese research, instruments, earthquake-resistant design, and study of the Sanriku tidal wave.

subfiles.title: Encouragement of Inventions
subfiles.about: The excerpt surveys incentives for Japanese inventors and research at the Chemical & Physical Research Institute.
subfiles.summary: Describes invention prizes, grants, selected patented inventions, and the institute’s research departments, factory, products, and patents.

subfiles.title: Co-operation in Research Is Essential to Today's Industry
subfiles.about: Mishida argues that Japanese industry needs stronger research cooperation, funding, and government coordination.
subfiles.summary: Surveys gaps in advanced textiles, dyes, materials, fuels, and manufacturing methods despite Japan’s rising industrial output. Calls for subsidized research, exchange among scientists, commercial use of discoveries, and controls on destructive competition.

subfiles.title: Government Laboratory, Osaka, Will Accomplish 12 Inventions
subfiles.about: The article outlines twelve Osaka laboratory developments approaching tests in model plants.
subfiles.summary: Projects include photographic lenses, carbon brushes, improved fish oil, cold-resistant lubricant, vanadium, synthetic and oil-resistant rubber, ceramics, ethylene, cellulose acetate, resin, and thymol. Successful processes were expected to be offered to firms for industrial use.

subfiles.title: Japan Engineering Congress Opening Third Session in Tokyo
subfiles.about: The article previews the third Japan Engineering Congress and its technical presentations.
subfiles.summary: Reports plans for roughly 6,000 participants and 743 papers across engineering fields. It names society presidents and previews research on fuels, acids, light metals, iron refining, ordnance, and shipbuilding.

subfiles.title: Patent Figures by Country, 1933–1935
subfiles.about: Tables list annual patent figures by country or territory for 1933, 1934, and 1935.
subfiles.summary: Country-by-country figures for three years, attributed to the United States Patent Office.

subfiles.title: 16,600 Patents Were Applied For, and 4,800 Recognized
subfiles.about: The article analyzes Japanese and foreign applications and registrations for industrial property.
subfiles.summary: Patent Bureau figures show rising Japanese patent activity and declining foreign applications from 1928 to 1935. Tables compare patents, utility models, designs, and trade marks, then examine mechanical, chemical, and electrical applications.

subfiles.title: Household Economy of Workpeople
subfiles.about: The excerpt compares income and expenditure of salaried and wage-earning families in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Based on Cabinet Statistical Bureau research for the year ending August 1934, it tabulates earnings, household spending, savings, and the shares devoted to necessities, social expenses, and culture.

subfiles.title: National Wealth of Japan Total 110 Billion Yen
subfiles.from: Contemporary Opinions on Current Topics; translated from Diamond
subfiles.about: The article estimates Japan’s national wealth and compares its distribution and historical growth.
subfiles.summary: Presents a Cabinet Statistical Bureau estimate of about 110 billion yen in national wealth at the end of 1930, broken down by assets and ownership. It compares prefectural and per-capita wealth and reviews earlier estimates reaching back to Perry’s visit.
